current.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
current.desc: In Bangladesh, the land with the highest density of population in the world (and the highest amount of corruption), the daily struggle to survive is fought everywhere, including the streets. Nowhere do people drive as brutally and recklessly as here. In Bangladesh you drive on the road like others drive with a bumper car: if you need space, you simply ram the car driving next to you. The police only came if there are fatalities. The biggest bottleneck in the transport system is the historical old town of Dhaka. Old Dhaka is a universe of its own, a world of bazaars in which every trade has its own quarter: there are streets of jewelers, sweets makers and fashionable tailors, and the vegetable wholesalers have their warehouses down at the port. The deliveries take place mostly on the river, the Buriganga River, a stinking cesspool. But the sold goods usually leave by land, and the customers also come by the land route – the Nawabpur Road. They generally come in buses or by rickshaw, where too many people are crammed into too little space. The traffic in Dhaka is everyday, normal madness. The film accompanies a rickshaw, a bus and a truck on their dangerous way through the streets of Dhaka and shows how it is possible to survive in what seems to be an incontrollable chaos.

next.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
next.desc: The “Adriatic Highway” is one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the world. The “technical masterwork” was built in the 1950s and 60s, at the time of Yugoslavian President Tito. Abounding in curves, the asphalt road stretches from Ankaran in Slovenia to Ulcinj in Montenegro. More than half of the road is in Croatia (659 km) and a quarter in Montenegro (125 km). Shorter segments lead through Slovenia; only nine kilometers are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all four countries of the former Yugoslavian Federation, the 1,200-kilometer-long highway remains the main thoroughfare of Adriatic tourism. For many travelers, the highway is the absolute dream road. In dizzying heights, it hugs the steep cliffs lining the Adriatic Sea, winds through coves and bays, gardens and stony fields. Wonderful views of the blue sea, green islands, bizarre cliffs and Mediterranean cities and towns are typical of the highway. But with its numerous curves, the dream road also harbors many dangers.

W nigdy wcześniej nie widzianym wywiadzie, były kamerdyner króla Karola, Grant Harrold, obecnie sensacja mediów społecznościowych, maluje intymny portret nowego monarchy, dając wgląd w człowieka, który zostanie koronowany na króla w pierwszej koronacji od 70 lat. Podczas gdy naród przygotowuje się do historycznej koronacji w maju 2023 roku, ten przełomowy i poruszający film ujawnia nową stronę króla Karola III i jego niezrównaną podróż w kierunku królewskości.

As a key trade port in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it was a gathering point for merchants and diplomats from all over the world. These buildings, mostly over 100 years old, stand witness to China's reconnection with the outside world.

current.title: Jodha Akbar
current.desc: Jodha Akbar est une histoire d'amour du seizième siècle qui raconte une saga de mariage politique de convenance entre un empereur moghol, Akbar, et une princesse rajput, Jodha. Mais c'est bien plus que cela : c'est le mariage des contrastes. Jalaluddin Mohammad (Akbar), qui avait hérité de l'empire moghol de son père Humayun à l'âge de 13 ans après la mort de ce dernier, avait été élevé presque comme un assassin entraîné par Bairam Khan, le commandant suprême de son père. Dur, rude, impitoyable et fier de chacune de ces facettes de sa personnalité, la seule chose qu'Akbar avait apprise était d'étendre son empire - au prix de la vie des autres - au prix des émotions - au prix de l'amour - un mot qu'il ne connaissait pas. En revanche, Jodha, la fille de Raja Bharmal, le roi rajput d'Amer (l'un des royaumes rajputs les plus riches de l'époque), valorisait chacune de ces émotions - elle valorisait la vie, même celle des oiseaux et des abeilles de son royaume. Elle détestait seulement les Moghols, qu'elle considérait comme des intrus sur ses terres, et voulait les chasser du territoire rajput, ainsi que leur empereur Jalaluddin, qu'elle haïssait de tout son cœur. Akbar ignorait qu'en épousant Jodha, la fougueuse princesse rajput, pour étendre son empire sur les terres rajputs, il entamerait en réalité un nouveau voyage - le voyage du véritable amour. Il découvrirait le cœur qu'il pensait ne jamais avoir - et il battrait pour sa véritable amante - Jodha.

Schnell führen die Ermittlungen ins Rotlichtmilieu der Stadt rund um den Hauptbahnhof. Traf Moshammer seinen Mörder etwa in der Szene, die er lange vor der Öffentlichkeit geheim halten wollte? current.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
current.desc: In Bangladesh, the land with the highest density of population in the world (and the highest amount of corruption), the daily struggle to survive is fought everywhere, including the streets. Nowhere do people drive as brutally and recklessly as here. In Bangladesh you drive on the road like others drive with a bumper car: if you need space, you simply ram the car driving next to you. The police only came if there are fatalities. The biggest bottleneck in the transport system is the historical old town of Dhaka. Old Dhaka is a universe of its own, a world of bazaars in which every trade has its own quarter: there are streets of jewelers, sweets makers and fashionable tailors, and the vegetable wholesalers have their warehouses down at the port. The deliveries take place mostly on the river, the Buriganga River, a stinking cesspool. But the sold goods usually leave by land, and the customers also come by the land route – the Nawabpur Road. They generally come in buses or by rickshaw, where too many people are crammed into too little space. The traffic in Dhaka is everyday, normal madness. The film accompanies a rickshaw, a bus and a truck on their dangerous way through the streets of Dhaka and shows how it is possible to survive in what seems to be an incontrollable chaos.

next.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
next.desc: The “Adriatic Highway” is one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the world. The “technical masterwork” was built in the 1950s and 60s, at the time of Yugoslavian President Tito. Abounding in curves, the asphalt road stretches from Ankaran in Slovenia to Ulcinj in Montenegro. More than half of the road is in Croatia (659 km) and a quarter in Montenegro (125 km). Shorter segments lead through Slovenia; only nine kilometers are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all four countries of the former Yugoslavian Federation, the 1,200-kilometer-long highway remains the main thoroughfare of Adriatic tourism. For many travelers, the highway is the absolute dream road. In dizzying heights, it hugs the steep cliffs lining the Adriatic Sea, winds through coves and bays, gardens and stony fields. Wonderful views of the blue sea, green islands, bizarre cliffs and Mediterranean cities and towns are typical of the highway. But with its numerous curves, the dream road also harbors many dangers.

current.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
current.desc: In Bangladesh, the land with the highest density of population in the world (and the highest amount of corruption), the daily struggle to survive is fought everywhere, including the streets. Nowhere do people drive as brutally and recklessly as here. In Bangladesh you drive on the road like others drive with a bumper car: if you need space, you simply ram the car driving next to you. The police only came if there are fatalities. The biggest bottleneck in the transport system is the historical old town of Dhaka. Old Dhaka is a universe of its own, a world of bazaars in which every trade has its own quarter: there are streets of jewelers, sweets makers and fashionable tailors, and the vegetable wholesalers have their warehouses down at the port. The deliveries take place mostly on the river, the Buriganga River, a stinking cesspool. But the sold goods usually leave by land, and the customers also come by the land route – the Nawabpur Road. They generally come in buses or by rickshaw, where too many people are crammed into too little space. The traffic in Dhaka is everyday, normal madness. The film accompanies a rickshaw, a bus and a truck on their dangerous way through the streets of Dhaka and shows how it is possible to survive in what seems to be an incontrollable chaos.

next.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
next.desc: The “Adriatic Highway” is one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the world. The “technical masterwork” was built in the 1950s and 60s, at the time of Yugoslavian President Tito. Abounding in curves, the asphalt road stretches from Ankaran in Slovenia to Ulcinj in Montenegro. More than half of the road is in Croatia (659 km) and a quarter in Montenegro (125 km). Shorter segments lead through Slovenia; only nine kilometers are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all four countries of the former Yugoslavian Federation, the 1,200-kilometer-long highway remains the main thoroughfare of Adriatic tourism. For many travelers, the highway is the absolute dream road. In dizzying heights, it hugs the steep cliffs lining the Adriatic Sea, winds through coves and bays, gardens and stony fields. Wonderful views of the blue sea, green islands, bizarre cliffs and Mediterranean cities and towns are typical of the highway. But with its numerous curves, the dream road also harbors many dangers.

current.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
current.desc: In Bangladesh, the land with the highest density of population in the world (and the highest amount of corruption), the daily struggle to survive is fought everywhere, including the streets. Nowhere do people drive as brutally and recklessly as here. In Bangladesh you drive on the road like others drive with a bumper car: if you need space, you simply ram the car driving next to you. The police only came if there are fatalities. The biggest bottleneck in the transport system is the historical old town of Dhaka. Old Dhaka is a universe of its own, a world of bazaars in which every trade has its own quarter: there are streets of jewelers, sweets makers and fashionable tailors, and the vegetable wholesalers have their warehouses down at the port. The deliveries take place mostly on the river, the Buriganga River, a stinking cesspool. But the sold goods usually leave by land, and the customers also come by the land route – the Nawabpur Road. They generally come in buses or by rickshaw, where too many people are crammed into too little space. The traffic in Dhaka is everyday, normal madness. The film accompanies a rickshaw, a bus and a truck on their dangerous way through the streets of Dhaka and shows how it is possible to survive in what seems to be an incontrollable chaos.

next.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
next.desc: The “Adriatic Highway” is one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the world. The “technical masterwork” was built in the 1950s and 60s, at the time of Yugoslavian President Tito. Abounding in curves, the asphalt road stretches from Ankaran in Slovenia to Ulcinj in Montenegro. More than half of the road is in Croatia (659 km) and a quarter in Montenegro (125 km). Shorter segments lead through Slovenia; only nine kilometers are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all four countries of the former Yugoslavian Federation, the 1,200-kilometer-long highway remains the main thoroughfare of Adriatic tourism. For many travelers, the highway is the absolute dream road. In dizzying heights, it hugs the steep cliffs lining the Adriatic Sea, winds through coves and bays, gardens and stony fields. Wonderful views of the blue sea, green islands, bizarre cliffs and Mediterranean cities and towns are typical of the highway. But with its numerous curves, the dream road also harbors many dangers.

current.title: Bootsraser im Visier: Tempolimits und Promillegrenzen im Schiffsverkehr
current.desc: Auf Europas Gewässern kommt es immer wieder zu schweren Bootsunfällen. Einige Freizeitkapitäne blenden aus, dass auch im Schiffsverkehr Tempolimits und Promillegrenzen gelten, und geben Gas. Nach einem tödlichen Unfall auf dem Gardasee im Sommer 2021 durch zwei deutsche Raser greift die italienische Polizei jetzt durch. Familie Garzarella lebt direkt am Gardasee im Städtchen Salò, regelmäßige Bootsausflüge gehörten da ganz selbstverständlich zum Leben dazu. Bis zum Abend des 19. Juni 2021. Der 37-jährige Umberto Garzarella ist mit seiner Freundin Greta auf dem See unterwegs, als plötzlich ein Sportboot auf sie zurast. Am Steuer: zwei Touristen aus München, vermutlich stark alkoholisiert. Mit rund 20 Knoten fahren sie viermal schneller als bei Dunkelheit erlaubt. Die Deutschen rammen das Boot des italienischen Paares und begehen anschließend Fahrerflucht. Umberto verblutete noch auf dem Holzboot, Greta wird ins Wasser geschleudert und kann am nächsten Tag nur tot geborgen werden. Die deutschen Raser kommen mit Haftstrafen von 4 Jahren und 6 Monaten sowie 2 Jahren und 11 Monaten glimpflich davon. Das milde Urteil sorgte in ganz Italien für Empörung, besonders bei den Bewohnern von Salò. Gemeinsam mit der Familie Garzarella erwirkten sie eine Verschärfung des italienischen Gesetzes. Seit 2023 gilt bei fahrlässiger Tötung auf dem Wasser das gleiche Strafmaß wie im Straßenverkehr. Für Geschwindigkeits- und Alkoholkontrollen auf dem Gardasee ist die italienische Finanzpolizei zuständig. Besonders zu schaffen machen ihr Touristen ohne Bootsführerschein, die mit Leihbooten über den See fahren. In Italien ist das möglich – in Kroatien hingegen braucht man für alle Motorboote unabhängig von der Größe eine Fahrerlaubnis. Hier wacht die Wasserschutzpolizei über die Einhaltung der Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung in Küstennähe, damit Badegäste sicher in der Adria schwimmen können. Eine »Arte Re:«-Reportage von SPIEGEL TV. (27.09.2024).

next.title: »Interview mit einem Killer«: Jack Unterweger (3) – Der Prostituiertenmörder
next.desc: Kurz nach dem Gerichtsurteil am 29. Juni 1994 erhängt sich Johann »Jack« Unterweger in seiner Zelle. Das Seil hat er mit dem gleichen Knoten befestigt, den die Ermittler auch an den Tatwerkzeugen bei mehreren ermordeten Frauen finden. War das eine Art von Geständnis? Im letzten Interview, das SPIEGEL TV mit ihm zwei Jahre zuvor im Gefängnis von Miami in den USA führt, streitet er die elf Morde ab. In unserer neuen Mini-Serie »Interview mit einem Killer« gehen wir dieser Frage und den Umständen seines Todes nach. Zu Gast sind Prof. Reinhard Haller, der Unterweger im späteren Gerichtsprozess psychiatrisch begutachtet hat. Und: Karin Assmann, damals SPIEGEL-TV-Korrespondentin in den USA. (10.11.2024).

current.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
current.desc: In Bangladesh, the land with the highest density of population in the world (and the highest amount of corruption), the daily struggle to survive is fought everywhere, including the streets. Nowhere do people drive as brutally and recklessly as here. In Bangladesh you drive on the road like others drive with a bumper car: if you need space, you simply ram the car driving next to you. The police only came if there are fatalities. The biggest bottleneck in the transport system is the historical old town of Dhaka. Old Dhaka is a universe of its own, a world of bazaars in which every trade has its own quarter: there are streets of jewelers, sweets makers and fashionable tailors, and the vegetable wholesalers have their warehouses down at the port. The deliveries take place mostly on the river, the Buriganga River, a stinking cesspool. But the sold goods usually leave by land, and the customers also come by the land route – the Nawabpur Road. They generally come in buses or by rickshaw, where too many people are crammed into too little space. The traffic in Dhaka is everyday, normal madness. The film accompanies a rickshaw, a bus and a truck on their dangerous way through the streets of Dhaka and shows how it is possible to survive in what seems to be an incontrollable chaos.

next.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
next.desc: The “Adriatic Highway” is one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the world. The “technical masterwork” was built in the 1950s and 60s, at the time of Yugoslavian President Tito. Abounding in curves, the asphalt road stretches from Ankaran in Slovenia to Ulcinj in Montenegro. More than half of the road is in Croatia (659 km) and a quarter in Montenegro (125 km). Shorter segments lead through Slovenia; only nine kilometers are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all four countries of the former Yugoslavian Federation, the 1,200-kilometer-long highway remains the main thoroughfare of Adriatic tourism. For many travelers, the highway is the absolute dream road. In dizzying heights, it hugs the steep cliffs lining the Adriatic Sea, winds through coves and bays, gardens and stony fields. Wonderful views of the blue sea, green islands, bizarre cliffs and Mediterranean cities and towns are typical of the highway. But with its numerous curves, the dream road also harbors many dangers.

current.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
current.desc: In Bangladesh, the land with the highest density of population in the world (and the highest amount of corruption), the daily struggle to survive is fought everywhere, including the streets. Nowhere do people drive as brutally and recklessly as here. In Bangladesh you drive on the road like others drive with a bumper car: if you need space, you simply ram the car driving next to you. The police only came if there are fatalities. The biggest bottleneck in the transport system is the historical old town of Dhaka. Old Dhaka is a universe of its own, a world of bazaars in which every trade has its own quarter: there are streets of jewelers, sweets makers and fashionable tailors, and the vegetable wholesalers have their warehouses down at the port. The deliveries take place mostly on the river, the Buriganga River, a stinking cesspool. But the sold goods usually leave by land, and the customers also come by the land route – the Nawabpur Road. They generally come in buses or by rickshaw, where too many people are crammed into too little space. The traffic in Dhaka is everyday, normal madness. The film accompanies a rickshaw, a bus and a truck on their dangerous way through the streets of Dhaka and shows how it is possible to survive in what seems to be an incontrollable chaos.

next.title: Hot Roads - The Worlds Most Dangerous Roads
next.desc: The “Adriatic Highway” is one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the world. The “technical masterwork” was built in the 1950s and 60s, at the time of Yugoslavian President Tito. Abounding in curves, the asphalt road stretches from Ankaran in Slovenia to Ulcinj in Montenegro. More than half of the road is in Croatia (659 km) and a quarter in Montenegro (125 km). Shorter segments lead through Slovenia; only nine kilometers are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all four countries of the former Yugoslavian Federation, the 1,200-kilometer-long highway remains the main thoroughfare of Adriatic tourism. For many travelers, the highway is the absolute dream road. In dizzying heights, it hugs the steep cliffs lining the Adriatic Sea, winds through coves and bays, gardens and stony fields. Wonderful views of the blue sea, green islands, bizarre cliffs and Mediterranean cities and towns are typical of the highway. But with its numerous curves, the dream road also harbors many dangers.
